Soy Santiago, estudiante de Ingeniería Eléctrica en la FING. Sé Python básico y estoy aprendiendo a trabajar con imágenes astronómicas. Es mi primer hackathon.

QUÉ BUSCAMOS

- Desarrollo web (HTML/CSS/JavaScript, etc)

- Python / procesamiento de datos o imágenes (NumPy, análisis de imágenes)

- Diseño / UX (opcional)

No hace falta ser experto: lo que más importa es la curiosidad y el compromiso.
summary:
Moving Pictures is a free, partly bilingual web application that makes NASA’s SPHEREx data accessible through an interactive visualization tool. Users can enter sky coordinates or select one of five featured objects. From nearby brown dwarfs to distant giant stars, users can retrieve and explore infrared observations from the SPHEREx archive. Difference images and comparisons with older WISE observations provide additional ways to identify subtle changes.
Through a simple web interface, users can explore infrared observations and watch aligned images come to life through animation. More than an image viewer, Moving Pictures is an invitation to explore a universe that cannot be seen with visible light alone. We want to inspire curiosity, make scientific data accessible, and show that anyone can take part in the discovery of our universe.
details:
Moving Pictures is a free, partly bilingual web application that allows anyone to explore real infrared images from NASA’s SPHEREx telescope and discover how celestial objects move or change over time. Inspired by the blinking technique used by Clyde Tombaugh to discover Pluto in 1930, our project turns astronomical data into an interactive and accessible experience. However, not all celestial objects reveal noticeable changes, some move very slowly or show only subtle variations, making their movement almost imperceptible between the first and subsequent observations. Even so, these small differences are part of what makes exploring the universe so fascinating.

Users can enter sky coordinates (RA/Dec) or select one of five featured objects: Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855−0714, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis. The application searches NASA/IPAC’s IRSA archive for available observations, downloads image cutouts, aligns them onto a common grid, and displays them as an animation. Users can explore different viewing modes, adjust the field of view and animation speed, and generate difference images to highlight positional changes. An optional image from the WISE mission (2010) provides a longer observational baseline, making subtle movements more noticeable.

The application also includes educational pages and short stories about each object, briefly explaining SPHEREx, infrared light, and the techniques astronomers use to study the universe. Our goal is to make real NASA data accessible to everyone, especially student curious people, encourage curiosity about astronomy and data science, and show that scientific exploration is not limited to specialists.

We developed the project using Python, Streamlit, Astropy, astroquery, reproject, NumPy, SciPy, and Pillow. We use SPHEREx and AllWISE data from NASA/IPAC IRSA, alongside astronomical information from SIMBAD.

What makes Moving Pictures creative is its combination of a discovery technique from the 1930s with modern space telescope observations. Since SPHEREx captures different infrared wavelengths, apparent brightness differences do not always represent actual changes over time. Rather than overlooking this, our application displays the wavelength of each observation and helps users understand the data. We also considered scientific accuracy, accessibility, download efficiency, and archive reliability, incorporating a demonstration mode for situations when the archive is unavailable.

For more information, visit our GitHub repository.
